```{r, echo=TRUE}
# --- 1. HELPER FUNCTIONS (for each type of data issue) ---

#' Introduce a percentage of missing values (NA) into random cells.
#' @param df The input dataframe.
#' @param p The percentage of total cells to replace with NA (e.g., 0.05 for 5%).
#' @return The dataframe with NAs introduced.
introduce_missing <- function(df, p) {
  if (p <= 0) return(df)
  n_total_cells <- prod(dim(df))
  n_missing <- floor(n_total_cells * p)
  
  # Get random row and column indices. Ensure no duplicates.
  indices <- sample(1:n_total_cells, n_missing)
  row_indices <- (indices - 1) %% nrow(df) + 1
  col_indices <- (indices - 1) %/% nrow(df) + 1
  
  for (i in 1:n_missing) {
    df[row_indices[i], col_indices[i]] <- NA
  }
  return(df)
}

#' Introduce outliers into a percentage of rows for all numeric columns.
#' @param df The input dataframe.
#' @param p The percentage of rows to turn into outliers (e.g., 0.03 for 3%).
#' @param magnitude The strength of the outlier (how many standard deviations from the mean).
#' @return The dataframe with outliers.
introduce_outliers <- function(df, p, magnitude = 5) {
  if (p <= 0) return(df)
  numeric_cols <- names(df)[sapply(df, is.numeric)]
  
  for (col in numeric_cols) {
    n_outliers <- floor(nrow(df) * p)
    if (n_outliers == 0) next
    
    rows_to_modify <- sample(1:nrow(df), n_outliers)
    col_mean <- mean(df[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
    col_sd <- sd(df[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)
    
    # Generate extreme values (can be high or low)
    outlier_values <- col_mean + (sample(c(-1, 1), n_outliers, replace = TRUE) * magnitude * col_sd)
    df[rows_to_modify, col] <- outlier_values
  }
  return(df)
}

#' Introduce right-skewness to a specified numeric column.
#' @param df The input dataframe.
#' @param target_col The name of the numeric column to skew.
#' @param skew_factor A value > 1 for right-skew (e.g., 2, 3). Value of 1 causes no change.
#' @return The dataframe with the skewed column.
introduce_skewness <- function(df, target_col, skew_factor) {
  if (skew_factor <= 1 || is.null(target_col)) return(df)
  if (!is.numeric(df[[target_col]])) {
    warning(paste("Skewness can only be applied to numeric columns. Skipping:", target_col))
    return(df)
  }
  
  x <- df[[target_col]]
  x_scaled <- (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  x_skewed <- x_scaled ^ skew_factor
  df[[target_col]] <- x_skewed * (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) + min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  return(df)
}

#' Introduce a percentage of duplicate rows.
#' @param df The input dataframe.
#' @param p The percentage of duplicate rows to add (e.g., 0.1 for 10%).
#' @return The dataframe with added duplicate rows.
introduce_duplicates <- function(df, p) {
  if (p <= 0) return(df)
  n_duplicates <- floor(nrow(df) * p)
  rows_to_duplicate <- df[sample(1:nrow(df), n_duplicates, replace = TRUE), ]
  return(rbind(df, rows_to_duplicate))
}


# --- 2. MASTER FUNCTION (to apply all corruptions) ---

#' Applies a series of data quality issues to any given dataframe.
#' @param input_df The original dataframe to corrupt.
#' @param p_missing Percentage of total cells to set to NA.
#' @param p_outliers Percentage of rows to receive outliers in numeric columns.
#' @param p_duplicates Percentage of duplicate rows to add.
#' @param skew_col (Optional) Name of the column to skew. If NULL, the script
#'   will automatically select the first numeric column it finds.
#' @param skew_factor The power to apply for skewness (e.g., 3 for strong right-skew).
#' @return A new dataframe containing all the introduced data issues.
corrupt_data_generic <- function(input_df, p_missing = 0.05, p_outliers = 0.03, p_duplicates = 0.10,
                                 skew_col = NULL, skew_factor = 3) {
  
  message("--- Starting Data Corruption Process ---")
  corrupted_df <- input_df
  
  # --- Step 1: Handle Skewness ---
  # If a specific column isn't provided, find the first numeric one automatically
  if (is.null(skew_col)) {
    numeric_cols <- names(corrupted_df)[sapply(corrupted_df, is.numeric)]
    if (length(numeric_cols) > 0) {
      skew_col <- numeric_cols[1] # Auto-select the first numeric column
      message(paste("No 'skew_col' provided. Automatically selected column '", skew_col, "' for skewness.", sep=""))
    } else {
      warning("Could not apply skewness: No numeric columns found in the dataset.")
      skew_col <- NULL # Ensure it's null if no suitable column is found
    }
  }
  corrupted_df <- introduce_skewness(corrupted_df, target_col = skew_col, skew_factor = skew_factor)
  
  # --- Step 2: Introduce Outliers ---
  message(paste("Introducing outliers to ~", p_outliers * 100, "% of rows in numeric columns.", sep=""))
  corrupted_df <- introduce_outliers(corrupted_df, p = p_outliers)
  
  # --- Step 3: Add Duplicates ---
  message(paste("Adding ~", p_duplicates * 100, "% duplicate rows.", sep=""))
  corrupted_df <- introduce_duplicates(corrupted_df, p = p_duplicates)
  
  # --- Step 4: Introduce Missing Values ---
  message(paste("Introducing missing values to ~", p_missing * 100, "% of total cells.", sep=""))
  corrupted_df <- introduce_missing(corrupted_df, p = p_missing)
  
  message("--- Corruption Process Complete ---")
  
  # Return the final corrupted dataframe
  return(corrupted_df)
}


# --- 3. EXAMPLE USAGE ---
# You would replace this with your own dataframe.

# Load the original, clean data
original_data <- my_data

# --- Run the master corruption function ---
# The function will automatically pick the first numeric column to skew.
corrupted_data <- corrupt_data_generic(
  input_df = original_data,
  p_missing = 0.05,
  p_outliers = 0.03,
  p_duplicates = 0.15,
  skew_factor = 3
)


# --- 4. VERIFICATION: Compare Original vs. Corrupted Data ---

# Original Data Summary
cat("\n\n--- ORIGINAL DATA SUMMARY ---\n")
print(paste("Dimensions:", paste(dim(original_data), collapse = " x ")))
print(paste("Total Missing Values:", sum(is.na(original_data))))
print(paste("Number of Duplicates:", sum(duplicated(original_data))))
print("Summary Statistics:")
print(summary(original_data))


# Corrupted Data Summary
cat("\n\n--- CORRUPTED DATA SUMMARY ---\n")
print(paste("Dimensions:", paste(dim(corrupted_data), collapse = " x ")))
print(paste("Total Missing Values:", sum(is.na(corrupted_data))))
print(paste("Number of Duplicates:", sum(duplicated(corrupted_data))))
print("Summary Statistics:")
print(summary(corrupted_data))

# Check skewness on the auto-selected column
# (The function printed which column it chose)
skewed_col_name <- names(original_data)[sapply(original_data, is.numeric)][1]
original_skew <- moments::skewness(original_data[[skewed_col_name]], na.rm = TRUE)
corrupted_skew <- moments::skewness(corrupted_data[[skewed_col_name]], na.rm = TRUE)

cat("\n--- Skewness Check on '", skewed_col_name, "' ---\n", sep = "")
print(paste("Original Skewness:", round(original_skew, 3)))
print(paste("Corrupted Skewness:", round(corrupted_skew, 3)))
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
method1_set <- final_invalid_removed

# Defining variable groups

  "daily_demand",

  "base_price",
  "demand_variability",
  "handling_score",
  "packaging_score",
  "discount_pct",
  "supplier_score"
)


count_variables <- c(
  "units_sold",
  "units_wasted",
  "initial_quantity",
  "temp_abuse_events",
  "days_until_expiry",
  "days_remaining_at_purchase",
  "shelf_life_days"
)

cat_variables <- c(
  "is_promoted",
  "was_spoiled",
  "quality_grade",
  "markdown_applied",
  "day_of_week",
  "is_weekend",
  "month",
  "region",
  "category"
)


library(e1071)
library(tibble)

skewness_table <- tibble(
  variable = num_variables,
  skewness = sapply(method1_set[num_variables], skewness, na.rm = TRUE)
)
skewness_table
mean_variables <- skewness_table$variable[
  abs(skewness_table$skewness) <= 0.5
]

median_variables <- skewness_table$variable[
  abs(skewness_table$skewness) > 0.5
]

mean_variables
median_variables



# Mean imputation
for (v in mean_variables) {
  method1_set[[v]][is.na(method1_set[[v]])] <-
    mean(method1_set[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Median imputation
for (v in median_variables) {
  method1_set[[v]][is.na(method1_set[[v]])] <-
    median(method1_set[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Count variables
for (v in count_variables) {
  method1_set[[v]][is.na(method1_set[[v]])] <-
    round(median(method1_set[[v]], na.rm = TRUE))
}

# Mode for categorical
get_mode <- function(x) {
  ux <- na.omit(x)
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(ux, ux)))]
}

for (v in cat_variables) {
  method1_set[[v]][is.na(method1_set[[v]])] <-
    get_mode(method1_set[[v]])
}

method1_set <- method1_set %>%
  mutate(
    handling_score = round(handling_score),
    packaging_score = round(packaging_score),
    supplier_score = round(supplier_score)
  )


colSums(is.na(method1_set))
summary(method1_set[mean_variables])
summary(method1_set[median_variables])
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# Method 2: Constraint based and Mice imputation
method2_set <- final_invalid_removed

# Initial quantity
initial_quantity_cbi <- method2_set %>%
  mutate(
    initial_quantity = if_else(
      is.na(initial_quantity) &
      !is.na(units_sold) &
      !is.na(units_wasted),
      units_sold + units_wasted,
      initial_quantity
    )
  )
# units sold
units_sold_cbi <- initial_quantity_cbi %>%
  mutate(
    units_sold = if_else(
      is.na(units_sold) &
      !is.na(initial_quantity) &
      !is.na(units_wasted),
      pmax(initial_quantity - units_wasted, 0),
      units_sold
    )
  )

# waste percent

waste_pct_cbi <- units_sold_cbi %>%
  mutate(
    waste_pct = if_else(
      is.na(waste_pct) &
      !is.na(units_wasted) &
      !is.na(initial_quantity) &
      initial_quantity > 0,
      (units_wasted / initial_quantity) * 100,
      waste_pct
    )
  )

# Revenue = selling_price × units_sold

revenue_cbi <- waste_pct_cbi %>%
  mutate(
    revenue = if_else(
      is.na(revenue) &
      !is.na(selling_price) &
      !is.na(units_sold),
      selling_price * units_sold,
      revenue
    )
  )
# waste cost

waste_cost_cbi <- revenue_cbi %>%
  mutate(
    waste_cost = if_else(
      is.na(waste_cost) &
      !is.na(cost_price) &
      !is.na(units_wasted),
      cost_price * units_wasted,
      waste_cost
    )
  )

# profit = revenue − (cost_price × units_sold) − waste_cost

profit_cbi <- waste_cost_cbi %>%
  mutate(
    profit = if_else(
      is.na(profit) &
      !is.na(revenue) &
      !is.na(cost_price) &
      !is.na(units_sold) &
      !is.na(waste_cost),
      revenue - (cost_price * units_sold) - waste_cost,
      profit
    )
  )
# Profit margin percent 
profit_margin_cbi <- profit_cbi %>%
  mutate(
    profit_margin_pct = if_else(
      is.na(profit_margin_pct) &
      !is.na(profit) &
      !is.na(revenue) &
      revenue > 0,
      (profit / revenue) * 100,
      profit_margin_pct
    )
  )
cbi_completed<- profit_margin_cbi

colSums(is.na(cbi_completed))

cbi_variables <- c(
  "initial_quantity",
  "units_sold",
  "waste_pct",
  "revenue",
  "waste_cost",
  "profit",
  "profit_margin_pct"
)
na_before_cbi <- colSums(is.na(method2_set[cbi_variables]))
na_before_cbi
na_after_cbi <- colSums(is.na(cbi_completed[cbi_variables]))
na_after_cbi
na_comparison <- data.frame(

  NA_before_CBI = na_before_cbi,
  NA_after_CBI  = na_after_cbi
)

na_comparison

# MICE imputation
library(mice)


mice_input <- cbi_completed %>%
  mutate(
    category = as.factor(category),
    region = as.factor(region),
    quality_grade = as.factor(quality_grade),
    is_promoted = as.factor(is_promoted),
    was_spoiled = as.factor(was_spoiled),
    markdown_applied = as.factor(markdown_applied),
    day_of_week = as.factor(day_of_week),
    is_weekend = as.factor(is_weekend),
    month = as.factor(month)
  )

mice_input <- mice_input %>%
  select(
    -record_id,
    -product_id,
    -product_name,
    -store_id,
    -supplier_id,
    -transaction_date,
    -expiration_date
  )

mice_imputation <- mice(
  mice_input,
  m = 1,          
  method = "pmm", 
  seed = 123
)

summary(mice_imputation)
method2_complete <- complete(mice_imputation)

method2_final <- cbind(
  cbi_completed[, c(
    "record_id",
    "product_id",
    "product_name",
    "store_id",
    "supplier_id",
    "transaction_date",
    "expiration_date"
  )],
  method2_complete
)

method2_final <- method2_final %>%
  mutate(
    days_until_expiry = if_else(
      is.na(days_until_expiry) &
      !is.na(shelf_life_days) &
      !is.na(days_remaining_at_purchase),
      shelf_life_days - days_remaining_at_purchase,
      days_until_expiry
    )
  )

colSums(is.na(method2_final))
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# COMPARISON


options(scipen = 999)

imp_vars <- c(
  "revenue",
  "profit",
  "daily_demand",
  "distribution_hours",
  "demand_variability"
)

options(scipen = 999)

for (v in imp_vars) {
  
  cat("\n==============================\n")
  cat("VARIABLE:", v, "\n")
  cat("==============================\n\n")
  
  # Missing values check
  cat("Missing Values:\n")
  cat("Original:", sum(is.na(final_invalid_removed[[v]])), "\n")
  cat("Method1 :", sum(is.na(method1_set[[v]])), "\n")
  cat("Method2 :", sum(is.na(method2_final[[v]])), "\n\n")
  
  # Identical check
  cat("Method1 vs Method2 identical?\n")
  print(identical(method1_set[[v]], method2_final[[v]]))
  
  cat("\nSummary Statistics\n")
  cat("Method1:\n")
  print(summary(method1_set[[v]]))
  
  cat("\nMethod2:\n")
  print(summary(method2_final[[v]]))
  
  # Plot comparison
  par(mfrow=c(1,3), mar=c(5,5,4,2))
  
  hist(final_invalid_removed[[v]],
       main=paste(v,"Original"),
       col="skyblue",
       xlab=v,
       border="white")
  
  hist(method1_set[[v]],
       main=paste(v,"Method1 (Mean/Median)"),
       col="orange",
       xlab=v,
       border="white")
  
  hist(method2_final[[v]],
       main=paste(v,"Method2 (MICE)"),
       col="lightgreen",
       xlab=v,
       border="white")
  
}

# Revenue: The variable revenue originally contained 7424 missing values, which were successfully imputed using both Mean/Median and MICE methods, resulting in no remaining missing values. The distributions after imputation remain strongly right-skewed, which is expected for revenue data because most products generate low to moderate sales, while a small number of products produce very high revenue, creating a long right tail. Since the overall distribution is preserved after imputation, it indicates that the imputation process did not distort the natural pattern of the data, and the MICE method provides slightly more realistic estimates by using relationships between variables.

# Profit : The variable profit originally contained 5919 missing values, which were successfully imputed using both the Mean/Median method (Method 1) and the MICE method (Method 2), resulting in no remaining missing values in the dataset. A comparison between the two methods shows that the imputed values are not identical, indicating that each method estimates missing values differently. While the mean profit remains almost the same (around 769) in both datasets, there are slight differences in the spread of the distribution, particularly in the third quartile and maximum values, where the MICE method produces slightly higher values. This suggests that MICE estimates missing values using relationships with other variables, rather than replacing them with a single central statistic like the mean or median. The histogram comparison also shows that the overall distribution pattern remains similar across the original and imputed datasets, indicating that the imputation process did not distort the natural structure of the data. Additionally, the presence of both negative and positive profit values is realistic, as some products may incur losses while others generate profit in real-world business scenarios. Overall, although both methods successfully handled missing values, the MICE method preserves variability and relationships in the data more effectively, making it a more realistic imputation approach.

# Daily demand : The variable daily_demand originally contained 7,292 missing values, which were successfully handled using both the Mean/Median imputation method (Method 1) and the MICE imputation method (Method 2), leaving no missing values in either dataset. The histogram comparison shows that the overall distribution remains right-skewed in all three cases (original, Method1, and Method2), indicating that most products have low to moderate daily demand, while only a small number of products experience very high demand, creating a long right tail. This pattern is normal and realistic for retail or supply chain data, where only a few items sell in large quantities. The summary statistics also show that the median demand remains the same (33) in both methods, while the mean and upper quartile values differ slightly, with MICE producing slightly higher estimates, suggesting that it captures relationships between variables when imputing missing values. Overall, since the shape of the distribution is preserved after imputation, it indicates that both methods filled the missing values without distorting the natural demand pattern of the data, while MICE provides slightly more variability and realistic estimates.
```

```{r, echo=TRUE}
# ===============================
# FINAL DATASET
# ===============================
data_final <- method2_final


# ===============================
# STEP 1: LOG TRANSFORMATION (for highly skewed variables)
# ===============================
library(e1071)

cat("Skewness BEFORE transformation:\n")
cat("  revenue    :", round(skewness(data_final$revenue,    na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("  waste_cost :", round(skewness(data_final$waste_cost, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("  profit     :", round(skewness(data_final$profit,     na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")

# Apply transformations
data_final$revenue    <- log1p(data_final$revenue)
data_final$waste_cost <- log1p(data_final$waste_cost)

# Profit can be negative → signed log
data_final$profit <- sign(data_final$profit) * log1p(abs(data_final$profit))

cat("\nSkewness AFTER transformation:\n")
cat("  revenue    :", round(skewness(data_final$revenue,    na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("  waste_cost :", round(skewness(data_final$waste_cost, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("  profit     :", round(skewness(data_final$profit,     na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")


# ===============================
# STEP 2: LOGICAL DATA CORRECTION
# ===============================

# Storage temperature realistic range
data_final$storage_temp <- ifelse(
  data_final$storage_temp < -5 | data_final$storage_temp > 10,
  NA,
  data_final$storage_temp
)


# ===============================
# STEP 3: WINSORIZATION (moderate outliers only)
# ===============================
library(ggplot2)

outlier_vars <- c(
  "daily_demand",
  "selling_price",
  "cost_price",
  "distribution_hours",
  "storage_temp",
  "temp_deviation"
)

for (v in outlier_vars) {
  
  Q1  <- quantile(data_final[[v]], 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  Q3  <- quantile(data_final[[v]], 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  IQR_val <- Q3 - Q1
  
  lower <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR_val
  upper <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR_val
  
  # Count before
  before <- sum(data_final[[v]] < lower | data_final[[v]] > upper, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Boxplot BEFORE
  p1 <- ggplot(data_final, aes(x = "", y = .data[[v]])) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue", color = "black",
                 outlier.colour = "red", outlier.size = 1.5) +
    labs(title = paste("Before Treatment:", v), y = v, x = "") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  print(p1)
  
  # Winsorization (capping)
  data_final[[v]] <- pmin(pmax(data_final[[v]], lower), upper)
  
  # Count after
  after <- sum(data_final[[v]] < lower | data_final[[v]] > upper, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Boxplot AFTER
  p2 <- ggplot(data_final, aes(x = "", y = .data[[v]])) +
    geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgreen", color = "black",
                 outlier.colour = "red", outlier.size = 1.5) +
    labs(title = paste("After Treatment:", v), y = v, x = "") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
  print(p2)
  
  cat("Variable:", v,
      "| Outliers BEFORE:", before,
      "| AFTER:", after, "\n")
}


# ===============================
# STEP 4: RE-IMPUTATION (after introducing NA)
# ===============================
library(mice)

data_final <- complete(mice(data_final, m = 1))


# ===============================
# STEP 5: FINAL CHECK
# ===============================
cat("\nFinal dataset dimensions:", nrow(data_final), "x", ncol(data_final), "\n")
cat("Total missing values remaining:", sum(is.na(data_final)), "\n")
```
